..
KEY MESSAGE 1...

The primary meteorological concern through mid to late week is a
train of mesoscale convective systems (MCSs) tracking
southeastward in northwesterly flow aloft around the
northeastern periphery of an amplifying ridge over the middle of
the country. While the individual MCSs are expected to maintain
a fairly progressive forward propagation, repetitive rounds of 
convection over the same corridors present a high-impact flash 
flooding and river flooding threat. 

Precipitable water values across the region will hover between
1.6 and 2.0 inches, representing the 90th to 95th percentile for
mid-August climatology. Confluent low-level westerly flow
intersecting an east-west oriented instability axis will support
hourly rainfall rates exceeding 2 to 4 inches per hour within 
deeper convective cores. While the current lush state of summer 
vegetation and intervening intervals allow soils to handle 
moderate water loads initially, localized extreme rainfall rates
can quickly exceed soil infiltration capacity. Any mesoscale 
backbuilding to the northwest or west, or any convective line 
orienting east-to-west parallel to steering flow, will produce 
prolonged dwell times of extreme rainfall rates, leading to 
localized life-threatening flash flooding regardless of 
antecedent soil conditions and with pre-moistening soils these 
threats will emerge event quicker. 

The threat is heightened during overnight hours when flash 
flooding is hardest to detect and react to. In coordination with
WPC, a Day 2 Moderate Risk for Excessive Rainfall has been 
placed over much of southeast Ohio and central West Virginia for
Tuesday. Given low confidence in the exact spatiotemporal track
of individual convective complexes due to upstream cold pool 
evolution and environmental modification, Flash Flood Watch 
issuance is deferred for now. However, a Flash Flood Watch 
encompassing most or all of the forecast area will almost 
certainly become necessary for the Tuesday through Thursday 
period. It is important to note that this scenario is not 
guaranteed to be widespread or even occur at all, but this setup
does leave the potential open to locally extreme flash flooding
impacts.

Multi-day cumulative precipitation totals of 3 to 6 inches
across larger river basins will drive significant rises, 
which could lead to river flooding, especially downstream of any
localized extreme rainfall totals.

The key takeaway is: Residents in hollows, floodplains, and low-
lying terrain should have multiple ways to receive warnings 
and have a plan of action to move to higher ground this week if
conditions warrant.

KEY MESSAGE 2...

A lesser but still substantial hazard involves severe weather
associated with the daily convective complexes through Wednesday
evening. The primary severe hazard will be damaging straight-
line wind gusts driven by consolidated MCS cold pools, though
bowing line segments and mesoscale boundary interactions will
also support an embedded tornado risk. The conditional threat
for more semi-discrete or discrete supercellular convection 
capable of all severe modes will be highest during peak heating 
late this afternoon (although this may remain north of us and 
already be congealed by the time it arrives) and again Wednesday
afternoon and evening.

Forecast soundings across the region display strong
thermodynamic support, with MLCAPE reaching 2000 to 3000J/kg 
and DCAPE values between 800 and 1200J/kg. Deep-layer 0-6km bulk
shear of 35 to 45KTs and 0-3km SRH near 100 to 200m2/s2 support
organized convective modes given discrete convection. 

In Appalachia and steep terrain, full tree canopy foliage 
combined with rapidly saturating topsoil lowers severe wind 
damage thresholds significantly. Sub-severe wind gusts of 40 to 
50 mph, especially when sustained over several minutes typical 
within cold pool driven gusts corridors, can easily uproot 
trees and knock down power lines. 

SPC maintains a Slight Risk for severe storms daily through 
Wednesday. An upgrade to risk levels may be warranted, 
especially on Tuesday/Wednesday as confidence increases.

For today, an ongoing MCS over Illinois and Indiana will weaken
as it approaches western counties late this morning. Resulting
morning cloud cover and stabilization across northern counties
may limit convective coverage there this afternoon (displacing
convective initiation farther north). This developing complex
could drop south overnight bringing forth the first round of
severe storms.

KEY MESSAGE 3...

A temporary break in this persistent fire hose of MCS pattern 
is possible by Friday night and the start of the weekend. Upper-
level ridging over the south-central states is forecast to 
shift slightly eastward, pushing the primary shortwave track and
moisture plume east of the central Appalachians. This 
transition will yield a trend toward drier and calmer conditions
for Friday night through Saturday.
